Lancets
LAN-sets
noun (plural)
From the Old French lancette, a little lance, diminutive of lance — Latin lancea. A small, sharp, double-edged blade; the surgeon’s instrument for opening a vein, and hence any small piercing blade.

Biblical Definition

The word stands at the heart of Carmel: the prophets of Baal, having called on their god from morning until noon with no answer, “cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them” (1Ki 18:28). Every feature of false religion is on display in that one verse. There is volume — they cried aloud. There is duration — from morning until the time of the evening sacrifice. There is technique — after their manner, an established liturgy of self-wounding. And there is escalation: when nothing happens, the answer is always to do more of it, harder, bloodier. What there is not, at any point, is a word from Baal, “for there was no voice, nor any that answered” (1Ki 18:26). Set beside this the God of Israel, whose prophet prays a prayer of some sixty words at the appointed hour of sacrifice, and the fire falls. Israel had been expressly forbidden this practice: “Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves” (Deu 14:1) — and note the ground of the prohibition. It is not that self-wounding is unseemly but that they are children. Sons do not have to bleed to get their Father’s attention.

Webster 1828 Definition

Small sharp double-edged blades, as of a surgeon; the instruments with which the prophets of Baal gashed themselves on Carmel.

LANCET, n. A small pointed surgical instrument, sharp on both edges, used in opening veins and tumours.

From the Old French lancette, a little lance; Latin lancea.

Any small piercing blade; in architecture, a narrow pointed window or arch.

1Ki 18:28: the prophets of Baal cut themselves with knives and lancets.

Such self-laceration was expressly forbidden to Israel (Lev 19:28; Deu 14:1).

Key Scripture

1Ki 18:26 — "And they took the bullock which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us. But there was no voice, nor any that answered. And they leaped upon the altar which was made."

1Ki 18:28 — "And they cried aloud , and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them."

1Ki 18:29 — "And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the time of the offering of the evening sacrifice, that there was neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded."

Deu 14:1 — "Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead."

Modern Corruption

Wherever acceptance with God is thought to depend on the intensity of the worshipper’s exertion — louder, longer, costlier, more painful — Carmel’s liturgy is being repeated with different instruments.

expand to see more

The corruption is worship measured by exertion. Baal’s prophets operated on a perfectly coherent principle: the god is reluctant, the worshipper must overcome that reluctance, and the currency of persuasion is intensity — volume, endurance, and finally blood. The instruments have changed; the principle is endemic. It appears in penance and self-flagellation, in the notion that a prayer must reach a certain pitch or length to be heard, in the sense that a service has failed unless the emotion ran high, and in the quiet conviction of many sincere believers that God attends to them in proportion to their fervour. All of it assumes a God who must be moved, and all of it puts the worshipper at the centre of the transaction.

Recover the plain sense: Elijah prayed briefly, at the hour God had already appointed for sacrifice, and asked expressly that the people might know that thou hast turned their heart back again — giving even their repentance to God. The fire fell on a soaked altar, in the evening, at the time of the offering, and it consumed the sacrifice rather than the prophet. That is the gospel pattern: the fire falls on the substitute. Deu 14:1 supplies the doctrine underneath — ye are the children of the LORD your God, therefore ye shall not cut yourselves. Sonship is the reason self-wounding is forbidden. A child who must bleed to be noticed has not understood his adoption.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French lancette, a little lance — a small piercing blade; the tool of Baal’s liturgy on Carmel.

expand to see more

Lancets — Old French lancette, diminutive of lance; Latin lancea.

A small double-edged blade, properly the surgeon’s vein-opener.

1Ki 18:28: used after their manner — an established liturgy of self-wounding.

Forbidden to Israel on the ground of sonship (Deu 14:1).

The contrast at Carmel is exertion against appointment: hours of blood, then a short prayer and fire.

Usage

"False religion escalates when unanswered; it has no category but more."

"Elijah prays at the appointed hour of sacrifice, and the fire consumes the substitute."

"Deu 14:1 forbids self-cutting because Israel are children, not suppliants."
